c.tagline: Candy-colored Dutch colonial waterfront, a floating bridge, and world-class reef diving.

taxi.fareNote: Curaçao has no Uber or ride-hailing; taxis (plates begin with 'TX') are unmetered with government-set zone fares — confirm the price before departing. US dollars are accepted alongside guilders.

emergency.note: 911 reaches police and fire, and 912 is the ambulance line; 112 also connects to emergency services. US dollars and English are widely used alongside guilders and Papiamento.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Avoid the quieter back streets of Otrobanda and outlying districts like Seru Fortuna after dark, where opportunistic street crime rises.
Never leave valuables in rental cars, especially at remote beaches, where break-ins are the most common tourist crime.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed historic heart on the east bank of Sint Anna Bay, where the candy-colored gabled facades of the Handelskade waterfront line the harbor; crammed with shops, the Floating Market, the 1674 synagogue, and museums, it is the walkable base for first-timers.

"The Other Side" across the Queen Emma pontoon bridge, a maze of twisting residential lanes and Curaçao's cultural quarter, home to the Rif Fort, the Kura Hulanda museum village, galleries, and the cruise terminal.

A restored 18th-century seafront district of pastel merchant mansions turned into boutique hotels, oceanfront bars, and some of the island's best restaurants and nightlife; the trendiest place to stay and go out.
A former Jewish merchant quarter of grand colorful mansions on the Waaigat, now an up-and-coming creative area known for bold street-art murals, design studios, and cafes.
A resort and beach zone on the southeast coast with calm coves, dive sites, beach clubs, and restaurants; a relaxed, water-focused base a short drive from the historic center.

water.note: Tap water is distilled seawater of excellent quality and completely safe.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 6:00 AM to about 10:00 PM on the main Willemstad corridors, with sparse service to outlying districts and reduced Sunday and holiday frequency.
transit.note: Curaçao has no rail or metro; public transport is the government ABC bus network of large buses plus privately run 'Konvoi' minibuses (marked BUS), radiating from the Otrobanda and Punda terminals. Most visitors rely on taxis or a rental car.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash — about ƒ2.20 (US$1.25) within Willemstad, more for outlying routes; US dollars are accepted. There is no rechargeable transit card.

car.idp: Not required for stays up to 3 months (US, Canadian, and EU licenses valid)

ferry: Free Otrobanda-Punda ferry when the bridge swings open

transit.m: Public bus (Konvoi/ABC) to Otrobanda terminal (~30-40 min, limited schedule)
Taxi to Willemstad (~15-20 min, fixed fare)

tip.r: A 10-12% service charge is often added to restaurant bills; if not, 10-15% is standard, and rounding up for taxis and housekeeping is appreciated.

food.name: Keshi Yena
food.desc: Curacao's national dish - a shell of Edam or Gouda baked around spiced chicken or beef with raisins, olives, capers and prunes.

places.name: Plasa Bieu
places.note: Old market hall where local cooks serve keshi yena and stews at communal tables, weekday lunch.

places.name: Rozendaels
places.note: Krioyo kitchen in a tropical garden known for keshi yena and slow-cooked local classics.

places.name: Marshe Nobo (New Market)
places.note: Working-day food hall of Curacaoan home cooks, cheap plates with funchi on the side.

food.name: Stoba (Goat or Beef Stew)
food.desc: Slow-simmered Krioyo stew of goat, beef or papaya in tomato, onion and island spice, served with funchi, rice and fried plantain.

places.name: Plasa Bieu
places.note: Kabritu and karni stoba ladled from the pot; the island's most authentic lunch counter.

places.name: Rozendaels
places.note: Karni stoba and galina di smor cooked the traditional way in a shaded garden.

places.name: Marshe Nobo (New Market)
places.note: Several vendors run stoba daily; go before 2pm while the pots are full.

food.name: Funchi and Tutu
food.desc: Cornmeal staples - funchi is a firm polenta cut into blocks or fried, tutu mixes it with black-eyed peas for a sweeter, denser side.

places.name: Plasa Bieu
places.note: Funchi and tutu come as standard with every stew plate here.

places.name: Marshe Nobo (New Market)
places.note: Home-style plates with fried funchi, plantain and okra stew.

places.name: Rozendaels
places.note: Serves funchi properly as the side to its Krioyo mains rather than fries.

food.name: Pastechi
food.desc: Deep-fried crescent pastry stuffed with cheese, spiced beef, chicken or tuna - the island breakfast, eaten hot from paper.

places.name: Marshe Nobo (New Market)
places.note: Morning pastechi counters fry to order; the cheese and beef fillings go first.

places.name: Plasa Bieu
places.note: Snack window alongside the stew stalls for pastechi and johnny cakes.

places.name: Punda Bakeries and Snack Trucks
places.note: Snack trucks and bakeries sell pastechi from early morning until sold out.

food.name: Sopi di Piska and Kadushi
food.desc: Island soups - clear fish soup rich with lime and root vegetables, and kadushi, a thick green soup made from cactus.

places.name: Plasa Bieu
places.note: Kadushi and fish soup appear on the daily rotation; ask what the pots hold.

places.name: Marshe Nobo (New Market)
places.note: Soup of the day served with funchi at market-hall prices.

places.name: Rozendaels
places.note: One of the easier places to try kadushi in a sit-down setting.

food.name: Piska Kora (Grilled Red Snapper)
food.desc: Whole red snapper fried or grilled with Creole sauce, served with funchi and plantain - the classic Curacao waterfront plate.

places.name: De Gouverneur
places.note: Terrace on the harbour facing the floating bridge; local fish plus keshi yena on the menu.

places.name: Plasa Bieu
places.note: Fried fish plates from the market cooks, whatever came in that morning.

places.name: Fisherman's Wharf, Marshe Bieu area
places.note: Floating market and fish stalls where the day's catch is sold and fried nearby.

food.name: Blue Curacao Liqueur
food.desc: The island's famous orange liqueur, distilled from the bitter laraha orange that only grows here - tasted at the historic estate distillery.

places.name: Landhuis Chobolobo
places.note: Home of the original Curacao of Curacao liqueur; free self-guided tour and tasting bar.

places.name: De Gouverneur
places.note: Harbour terrace pouring blue Curacao cocktails with the bridge in view.

places.name: Pietermaai District Bars
places.note: Restored colonial quarter with the liveliest cocktail bars in Willemstad.

food.name: Awa di Lamunchi and Local Beer
food.desc: Awa di lamunchi is the island lime drink served everywhere; alongside it, cold Amstel Bright is the standard Curacao beach beer.

places.name: Plasa Bieu
places.note: Home-made awa di lamunchi and tamarind juice served in jugs with lunch.

places.name: Marshe Nobo (New Market)
places.note: Fresh fruit-juice counters press lime, soursop and tamarind drinks daily.

places.name: Pietermaai District Bars
places.note: Waterside bars for a cold Amstel Bright at sunset.

landmarks: Handelskade Waterfront
The Caribbean's most photographed street, a candy-coloured row of Dutch colonial facades lining Punda's harbourfront along the Sint Anna Bay.
Queen Emma Bridge
The swinging 'Old Lady', a 19th-century floating pontoon bridge that pivots open for ships while pedestrians cross between Punda and Otrobanda.
Mikvé Israel-Emanuel Synagogue
The oldest synagogue in continuous use in the Americas, consecrated in 1732, famous for its sand-covered floors and serene courtyard museum.
Fort Amsterdam
The ochre-walled 17th-century fort at the harbour mouth, seat of Curaçao's government, with a church still bearing a cannonball in its wall.
Rif Fort
A massive 1828 harbour fortress in Otrobanda whose vaulted casemates now house waterfront restaurants, shops and sunset ramparts, part of the UNESCO zone.
Floating Market
Venezuelan schooners moored along the Waaigat canal have sold fresh fish, mangoes and plantains from their decks for over a century.
Otrobanda Street Art and Historic Quarter
A maze of restored colonial alleys and monumental murals across the bay, where Kaya Kaya festival energy meets old Willemstad architecture.
Kura Hulanda Museum
A moving anthropological museum in a restored merchant quarter, unflinchingly documenting the transatlantic slave trade and African heritage of the Caribbean.
Queen Juliana Bridge
One of the Caribbean's highest bridges vaults 56 metres over Sint Anna Bay, giving drivers a spectacular panorama of Willemstad's coloured rooftops.
Fort Nassau
An 18th-century fort on a hilltop overlooking Willemstad's harbor, its ramparts converted into a restaurant terrace with panoramic views over the city and sea.

train.note: Curaçao has no railway. Arrive by air into Curaçao International Airport, which has direct flights from Amsterdam, Miami and across the Caribbean, or by cruise ship. There is no rail anywhere in the Dutch Caribbean.

bus.note: No international coaches. Autobusbedrijf Curaçao runs the large blue buses from the Otrobanda and Punda terminals across the island, supplemented by konvoi minibuses that leave when full and cover the same routes more frequently. Fares are cheap and paid in cash on board.

intl.to: Otrobanda & Punda (Curaçao) - across St Anna Bay
intl.op: Willemstad free pedestrian ferry — no ticket required

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international ferry - travel between the ABC islands is by air. Within Willemstad, the free pedestrian ferry across St Anna Bay is essential transport whenever the Queen Emma pontoon bridge swings open for shipping, which happens several times a day. Boats to Klein Curaçao are day-trip excursions.

half.name: Hato Caves
half.blurb: Limestone caverns just north of town glittering with stalactites, hidden pools and ancient Amerindian petroglyphs, plus resident long-nose bats.
